scenes.text: In thirteenth-century Byzantium, a physician's handbook prescribes a drug called alyssos. Which plant is that?
Modern readings rest on dictionaries that disagree, so a lab can test the wrong species. In twenty twenty-four, experts scored fifty names by hand, one label each.
For alyssos, they rated Fibigia a strong fit, and Scutellaria a weak one. Pick the plant with a known use, and you pick the one that fits the text less well.
Materia Incerta shows how sure an identification is, and which compounds survive the doubt.
First, every plant name is hidden. Then a language model compares each ancient detail with a modern flora, and it has to quote both texts, or the match doesn't count.
Here it is, live. Ten comparisons on Dioscorides' original Greek, answered by Qwen three on Nebius in under fourteen seconds.
Blind to the names, the model gives Fibigia three partial fits and one conflict, and Scutellaria one fit and two conflicts. The same direction as the experts.
For every name, a ranked list with its evidence, how stable it is, and which compounds hold.
Next, all fifty names against the expert benchmark. Materia Incerta: lab time for the compounds that survive identification doubt.
